analysis.one_liner: Bans PAC money in federal elections, limits congressional donations to in-state individuals, and bans gifts to House members.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 1995 with 21 Republican cosponsors, the Clean Congress Act never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Clean Congress Act would have rewritten federal campaign finance rules to strip organized money out of elections: no candidate could take money from political action committees, congressional candidates could accept money only from individuals who live in their own state and from party committees, and candidates could lend their own campaigns no more than $5,000. It also would have extended the ban on members' taxpayer-funded mass mailings from 60 to 90 days before an election, and imposed a blanket ban on gifts, meals, and reimbursed travel for House members, officers, and staff, with fines of up to three times the value of anything accepted.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who would no longer compete against organized PAC money in federal elections, and candidates who run on small individual donations from people actually living in their state. Members of the public would also gain from a House whose members cannot accept gifts, meals, or lobbyist-paid travel from the interests they regulate.

how_it_helps.text: Bans all contributions to federal candidates from anyone except individual people and political party committees, which would eliminate corporate, union, and trade-association PAC money from House, Senate, and presidential races.

Goes further for congressional races: Senate and House candidates could accept money only from party committees and from individuals who reside in the state where the election is held, cutting off out-of-state and organized-money funding.

Eliminates the separate, higher contribution limits that multicandidate PACs enjoy, and extends the annual contribution limit to every non-party giver, closing a loophole that let PACs give more per cycle than an individual could.

Bans House members, officers, and employees from accepting gifts, meal or entertainment reimbursements, and travel paid by anyone other than a relative or personal friend, and penalizes violations with a fine of one to three times the value of what was accepted.

Extends the ban on franked (taxpayer-funded) mass mailings by members from 60 to 90 days before an election, shrinking the window in which incumbents can use public money to reach voters as re-election nears.
Caps candidates' personal loans to their own campaigns at $5,000 per election, limiting one way wealthy self-funders can outspend opponents.

analysis.who_pays: Corporate, union, and trade-association PACs, which would lose their main channel for funding federal candidates, and lobbying and government-relations interests, which would lose gifts, meals, and paid travel as tools for access. Party committees gain the only non-individual funding channel. Congressional candidates lose out-of-state and PAC money, and members lose pre-election franked mail and gift-funded perks.
analysis.who_pays_short: PACs, lobbying firms, and party committees' rivals

drawbacks.text: The gift ban is shot through with exceptions: meals and entertainment at 'widely attended gatherings' such as receptions and charity events are allowed, and gifts or meals framed as 'personal friendship' are permitted, with an Ethics Committee waiver needed only above $250 — leaving lobbyists room to keep spending on members.

Restricting congressional candidates to in-state individual donors could cut off small donations from supporters who live across a state line, moved recently, or want to back a candidate elsewhere, and would push more money through national party committees, which become the only non-individual funding channel left standing.

The bill caps candidates' personal loans to their campaigns but is silent on outright personal contributions beyond applying the general annual limit, so a wealthy candidate's self-funding is narrowed rather than eliminated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's costs fall almost entirely on organized money in politics — PACs, lobbying firms, and donors who fund candidates outside their own state — rather than on ordinary people, which is the point of the bill. Its genuine weaknesses are design ones: the gift ban's exceptions for widely attended events and 'friendship' gifts would leave familiar loopholes open, and routing all non-individual money through party committees would concentrate fundraising power in the parties. On balance it is a far-reaching anti-corruption package whose worst feature is that it was never allowed to be debated, let alone improved.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced and later to two subcommittees; none of them ever acted on it, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda Smith of Washington introduced the Clean Congress Act on July 19, 1995, joined by four original cosponsors — Reps. Brownback, Fox, Metcalf, and Tate.

The same day, the Speaker referred it to four committees — House Oversight, Rules, Government Reform and Oversight, and Standards of Official Conduct — 'for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker,' meaning no committee was given a deadline to act.

In the following weeks it was sent down to the Subcommittee on Postal Service (July 26) and the Subcommittee on Rules and Organization of the House (September 5), where campaign finance and House-rules provisions typically go to wait.

No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place. By the time the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, the bill had been pending for nearly a year and a half with 21 Republican cosponsors and nothing to show for it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs and the lobbying industry kept their funding and access channels untouched, and members of Congress kept their gift, meal, and travel perks and their 90-day pre-election mailing window, because no committee or the Speaker ever let the bill advance.

for.name: Rep. Linda Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Clean Congress Act banning PAC money, out-of-state contributions, and House gifts; she was known for refusing PAC money to her own campaign.

for.name: Reps. Sam Brownback, Jon Fox, Jack Metcalf, and Randy Tate
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors the day the bill was introduced.

for.name: 17 additional House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after introduction, bringing the total to 21 Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Oversight, Rules, Government Reform and Oversight, and Standards of Official Conduct Committees
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from July 1995 onward without a single hearing, markup, or vote; it was parked in the Postal Service and Rules and Organization subcommittees and never reported out.

against.name: Speaker Newt Gingrich
against.what_they_did: Held the power to set committee deadlines and the floor calendar; the bill's referral left timing 'to be subsequently determined by the Speaker,' and no floor action was ever scheduled. Reporting from the period records his leadership's lack of interest in campaign finance restrictions.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter in the record was a Republican — the sponsor plus 21 cosponsors, with no Democratic cosponsors — but because the bill never reached a vote, no one ever had to go on record for or against it.

industries.note: The bill bans PAC contributions to all federal candidates and strips multicandidate PACs of their higher limits, eliminating the main vehicle through which organized business and labor money reaches lawmakers. PACs exist to pool money for influence over the people who write the rules, so their loss is the public's gain in this bill.

A blanket ban on gifts, meal and entertainment reimbursements, and reimbursed travel for House members and staff — enforced by fines of one to three times the value received — would cut off the hospitality-and-travel toolkit that buys access. The exceptions for widely attended gatherings and personal-friendship gifts soften but do not remove the hit.

With PACs banned and individual donors the only other allowed source, party committees become the only non-individual funding channel for federal candidates, concentrating fundraising power in party machinery. That strengthens parties relative to both outside groups and grassroots candidates.
